context: This comment responds to a Hacker News discussion about a wave of AI-discovered software vulnerabilities, zero-days and CVEs exposing decades of technical debt. It argues that complaints about the disruption miss the benefit: software will eventually be more secure.

This comment discusses the HTTP2Shell/Brotli2Shell vulnerability, arguing it was worse than PHP2Shell, and cites its disclosure timeline: eight years in the code, eight months unreleased despite a Git fix, and multiple researchers reporting it.

AI-driven discovery of software vulnerabilities and CVEs, with a flood of new 0-day patches. The comment hopes that AI is also surfacing backdoors and 0-days held by nation states and spyware firms like Pegasus, and that the resulting patching will leave software more robust.

Discussion of AI-driven discovery of security vulnerabilities and technical debt in software, and whether compliance certifications like ISO 27001 reliably reflect real security. The comment argues that such certifications are easy to game, and that AI tools are changing how companies weigh the risk of relying on them.

AI-assisted cleanup of legacy technical debt in codebases, discussed in a thread about AI forcing developers to pay off decades of accumulated code debt and security vulnerabilities. The commenter says AI lowered the cost of fixing 5-7 year old issues, with verification through existing tests.

A Hacker News discussion on AI-driven vulnerability discovery forcing developers to fix decades of accumulated technical debt. The commenter, a non-CS reader, asks whether Gödel's incompleteness theorem, via the tortoise-and-rabbit record player parable in *Gödel, Escher, Bach*, implies that no perfectly secure or unbreakable software can exist.

AI-driven discovery of security vulnerabilities and old technical debt in codebases, following the PHP2Shell and HTTP2Shell disclosures. The comment asks whether this is genuinely paying down debt or creating an endless treadmill of fix-work to stay ahead of hostile AI exploits.

A Hacker News discussion on whether AI-assisted coding is paying down decades of technical debt or creating new debt. This comment describes using AI to quickly build throwaway scripts and prototypes, then using it to carefully refine real projects, arguing that the slower, deliberate design debate with the AI yields a sounder foundation.

AI-driven vulnerability discovery and patching in software security, questioning whether a flood of AI-found bugs matters if AI can also fix them. The commenter notes that prompting a model to find more bugs almost always succeeds.

AI-driven discovery of legacy software vulnerabilities and the resulting wave of zero-days and CVEs. The commenter, who invested in an AI security seed fund, argues that the main challenge is convincing non-technical management to prioritize security and that red-team firms can help communicate these risks.

AI-assisted coding is adding new technical debt to software codebases faster than teams can pay down existing debt. This comment, a reply within a discussion of AI-driven vulnerability discovery and fixing old technical debt, responds to that broader topic.

AI-assisted patching of legacy code and accumulated technical debt, as discussed in a thread on AI forcing the industry to fix decades of software debt. The comment argues AI has removed excuses for avoiding that cleanup, and notes that legacy stacks like JSP web servers also carry bugs and dependency risks.

AI-assisted coding and the thread's broader debate over whether AI tools are paying down or creating technical debt. The comment argues that AI generates a new kind of debt, where no one on the team understands the code being written and developers simply trust the machine's output.

AI-assisted fixing of technical debt and security vulnerabilities in codebases, and whether AI-generated patches are reliable. The commenter warns that AI-written fixes can be brittle, have non-obvious failure cases, and invent workarounds, so careful code review is still needed.

This comment argues that software evolution follows a least-action-like principle, settling into local "energy wells" of complexity that make radical foundational redesigns rare. It cites the internet's hourglass model and the staying power of narrow waist layers like x86 as examples.

AI-assisted software development, specifically how AI tools may finally deliver long-promised practices like CI/CD (continuous integration and delivery) and their efficiency benefits. The comment suggests AI is fulfilling past promises from software evangelists.

Reply in a thread about AI-driven discovery of software vulnerabilities and technical debt, suggesting that the "Black October" information security event is only a beginning and speculating about a follow-on wave of exploits named "Vantablack November."

AI-driven code analysis tools for finding and fixing security vulnerabilities, in the context of a thread about a wave of AI-discovered bugs and 0-days forcing the industry to pay down decades of technical debt. The comment predicts that advanced AI analysis will shrink the attack surface, though not eliminate all bugs.

This comment responds to an article about AI-driven vulnerability discovery exposing decades of software technical debt, such as the PHP2Shell bug. It argues that C/C++ is nearing decline, that Rust's memory safety helps, that multithreaded code is too hard for most developers, and that the coming wave of 0-days will ultimately yield more secure software.

Commenter argues that maintaining code is an ordinary cost of ownership, like a house or car, and objects to the term "technical debt" as vague and negatively loaded. This is part of a discussion on whether AI is forcing payoff of decades of accumulated software technical debt and security vulnerabilities.

AI-assisted code cleanup removing 80,000 lines of code without breaking anything, in a codebase where much of the code had been AI-generated only months earlier. Part of a discussion on AI's effect on technical debt and code quality.

AI-generated code and its effect on software technical debt, as discussed in a thread on the AI-driven wave of vulnerability discoveries and patching. The comment proposes comparing the technical debt of code written since 2026 with code from the prior 40 years to measure AI's impact, and asks whether sloppy but bug-free AI code beats the alternative.

AI-driven discovery of security vulnerabilities and long-neglected technical debt in software codebases, following a wave of 0-days and CVEs. The comment argues AI is not only exposing this debt but also helping pay it down, predicting a rough transition that ends with stronger software.

AI coding model "Opus 5.5" becoming more capable in September, which led a team to be flooded with old technical debt it identified and recommended fixing. Fixing the backlog took two to three frantic weeks.

Commenter describes moving away from large AI-assisted codebases toward minimal, purpose-built software, such as AI-assisted microkernels and a webserver that only does what's needed, rather than relying on bloated dependencies. The thread concerns AI-driven vulnerability discovery and technical debt.

The comment discusses how AI-driven vulnerability discovery is overwhelming bug bounty programs, with duplicate reports and some programs shutting down. It suggests formal verification, as Anthropic has proposed, as a future path for securing widely used software.

A commenter in a thread about AI forcing developers to pay down decades of technical debt and security vulnerabilities argues that computing's whole paradigm needs replacing. They propose modeling tasks as isolated, composable Nix flake workflows, with dependency updates checked by security-scanner subgraphs.

The comment explains the mechanics of a vulnerability in musl libc's crypt() function combined with OpenSSH's password validation under sshd. It describes how returning "*" as an error token, when OpenSSH passes a different hash for disabled accounts, lets a long password bypass login authentication.

A Hacker News discussion on AI-discovered software vulnerabilities and the growing pile of technical debt they expose, including the PHP2Shell and HTTP2Shell bugs. This comment argues that the defenders now have the same AI tools as attackers, so all developers should use LLMs to security-test software, and insecure systems should fail an LLM stress test.

The comment concerns the musl libc crypt() bug that let OpenSSH logins succeed with long passwords on accounts whose shadow hash was "*". It argues that using "*" as a magic string for both "no password" and "hashing error" is in-band signaling, and that errors should be exceptions or Result types instead.

The comment analyzes a 2026 OpenSSH/musl vulnerability in which musl's crypt() returns "*" on error, and explains that the SHA-256 code path in musl lacks the workaround present in its DES path. It argues that sshd's missing salt handling, not just musl, is responsible.

A Hacker News discussion on AI-driven discovery of long-hidden software vulnerabilities (such as PHP2Shell and Brotli2Shell) and whether "technical debt" framing blames developers unfairly. The comment argues that software complexity and organizational incentives, not negligence, explain why such flaws went unnoticed for decades.

The comment reacts to the musl libc crypt() vulnerability, where returning "*" as an error token let OpenSSH logins succeed for disabled accounts with long passwords. It criticizes musl's "convenient" changes to core crypto functions made without sufficient auditing, which it says damaged musl's reputation.

This comment advises against "magic strings" in crypto and system code, such as the "*" that musl's crypt() returned as an error marker and that was abused in the OpenSSH login bypass. It suggests returning a failure value instead, or using a random valid hash or an unmistakable placeholder like "--ACCOUNT-HAS-NO-PASSWORD--".

Former network equipment QA lead describes years of vendor testing, including oversized password and CLI input sanity tests, and says they caught bugs but never one like the musl crypt() SSH login flaw, where a long password bypassed authentication.

The comment questions the MITRE/NVD score of 8.1 with "high attack complexity" for CVE-2026-123158, a musl crypt() flaw in OpenSSH logins on Alpine. It argues that exploitation only requires an SSH login attempt with a password over 256 characters.

The comment responds to the musl libc crypt() bug that let OpenSSH sshd accept any long password for accounts with a "*" hash, a bug that is more than 20 years old in the sense of longstanding design. It argues that long-established software is not automatically more secure, since accumulated cruft and rarely scrutinized options can hide flaws.

This comment argues that software should fail loudly rather than use silent compatibility hacks, citing the musl crypt() "*" error return bug. It draws a parallel to Microsoft's Vista UAC, which exposed badly behaved applications and pushed vendors to fix them.

The comment asks whether anyone has reproduced the musl crypt() vulnerability in OpenSSH on Alpine Linux, where a password over 256 characters bypasses login. It reports failed attempts on the official Alpine Docker image with root password login enabled, using "!" and "*" shadow entries, on OpenSSH 10.3p1 and Alpine 3.24.

The comment reports reproducing a musl/OpenSSH password-authentication bug on Alpine 3.23.7 with OpenSSH 10.2p1, where a crypt() error token ("*") lets long passwords bypass login checks. It notes that PermitRootLogin's default of disallowing root password logins since 2015 may explain why the flaw went unnoticed.

This comment concerns the musl libc crypt() vulnerability in OpenSSH sshd on Alpine Linux, where a long password bypasses authentication for accounts with a "*" shadow hash. It summarizes the conditions needed to exploit it, including PermitRootLogin defaults and the two-attempt sequence, and whether "!" locked accounts are affected.

This comment recalls a Vancouver Public Library terminal in the 1990s, where a very long input line gave access to a Unix shell with overly permissive file permissions. It draws a parallel to the musl/OpenSSH crypt() long-password bug discussed in the thread, which similarly relies on oversized input.

The comment compares the musl crypt() and OpenSSH password-check bug, where passwords over 256 characters trigger a "*" error return that matches a disabled account's hash, to Luigi Auriemma's early-2000s Quake 3 and Jedi Academy exploits that used long strings of "A" characters.

The comment asks about the page presenting the musl/OpenSSH crypt() vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) with commits and code excerpts styled like classic Windows screenshots, and whether the tool used to generate those linked images is publicly available or custom-built.

The comment asks whether embedded router firmware such as OpenWRT and AsusWRT is affected by the musl crypt() bug that allows SSH login with long passwords. It notes these systems typically use Dropbear rather than OpenSSH.

The comment reacts to the musl libc vulnerability in crypt(), where a password over 256 bytes makes crypt() return "*" as an error marker. That in-band error value, which can match a locked account's hash in OpenSSH, is questioned as a design choice.

The comment is about the musl libc crypt() bug that let SSH logins succeed with overlong passwords on Alpine-style systems using OpenSSH. It argues that SSH servers should disable password authentication and be hardened, since bots quickly scan even non-standard ports.

The comment reacts to the musl crypt() bug, where a "*" error token let OpenSSH password checks succeed against disabled accounts. It argues that verification checks must be enforced within the execution path itself, since a separate boolean check can be bypassed.

The comment is about the musl libc `crypt()` bug that let OpenSSH logins succeed with overlong passwords on accounts with "*" hashes. It praises the flaw as a chain of simple logic errors rather than a memory-safety bug, where each step seems reasonable on its own.

The comment asks which real-world systems combine musl libc, OpenSSH sshd with password authentication, and no PAM, the configuration needed for the musl crypt() vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) to be exploitable. It questions whether anything beyond hypothetical Alpine setups is actually affected.

This comment questions whether musl libc broke POSIX standards by having its crypt() function return "*" as an error token instead of NULL. The surprise is that musl is known for strict standards compliance. It follows the discussion of the OpenSSH login bypass on musl-based systems.

The comment concerns the OpenSSH/musl libc `crypt()` vulnerability, where passwords over 256 characters can cause login with disabled-password accounts (hash "*"). It says the flaw affects musl systems without PAM and suggests mitigations: disabling PasswordAuthentication or applying the update.

The comment discusses a vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux, where any password over 256 characters is accepted during SSH login. It speculates that common fuzzers would have caught this, suggesting OpenSSH was never fuzzed on musl.

The comment reacts to the musl libc `crypt()` bug, where a password over 256 bytes made it return "*" as an error token, letting OpenSSH logins succeed for accounts with "*" hashes. It is a broader remark about the current wave of security bugs and better tools for writing secure software.

The comment suggests that the musl libc vulnerability, where crypt() returns "*" as an error token that can match a disabled account's hash and let OpenSSH sshd accept a long password, may be an intentional backdoor rather than an accident.

This comment responds to the musl libc crypt() bug, where returning "*" as an error token let sshd accept logins with long passwords on Alpine systems. It proposes an extreme global response: shutting down non-critical internet-facing services and banning C programmers from the profession.

The comment reacts to the musl libc `crypt()` bug, where returning "*" as an error token let OpenSSH sshd accept any password over 256 characters for accounts with "*" hashes. It suggests that a run of such security flaws in widely used software looks more like deliberately planted backdoors than accidents.

Anthropic's Claude signup and account-cancellation concerns, from a developer who hasn't yet adopted AI coding agents. They're stalled because Claude's verification emails never reach their domain, which uses Constant Contact, and they want suggestions for working around it.

A blog post describing a musl libc crypt() bug that let OpenSSH password logins succeed with overlong passwords on accounts with a "*" hash. The commenter contrasts it with AI-generated content, praising the write-up as human-written after LLMs were used to find the bug.

This HN comment describes a developer's workflow for managing 10-100 concurrent AI coding agents across many projects, from ticket to plan to worktree implementation to merge, with mobile access. It mentions rev0.codes, a custom tool the author built for this.

This HN comment describes a minimalist workflow for AI coding agents: using Claude's IDE with Opus 5.5 at medium effort, dropping custom skills, and specifying what "complete" looks like. It also suggests running at least five parallel tasks to keep agents busy.

This comment describes a multi-model AI coding workflow that uses Claude for planning, Codex for review, and DeepSeek for implementation, orchestrated through a custom skill and the Pi harness with herdr and Collie for managing agents.

This comment describes a commenter's unusual personal computer setup for AI coding agents: a kiosk-mode browser with a local Weston server streamed over VNC, code-server instead of VS Code, and pi agents run from the terminal, using browser DevTools MCP.

This comment describes a multi-model AI coding setup that uses the open-source Redis-backed "nova-bus" message bus and a "nova-sprint" card system to coordinate many agents across 20 machines. It also notes that the combined code needs manual cleanup and that cross-model review improves quality.

This HN comment describes a personal AI coding setup: Claude Code running Opus 5.5 under separate Linux user accounts for sandboxing, with Obsidian plan workflows, QuickAdd commands, and tmux sessions per project.

A Hacker News thread on AI agentic coding setups, where a commenter says they use only the DeepSeek Flash API through a DeepSeek harness to build apps in Rust, Swift, and Node, including a custom language and compiler. They report no hand-written code since May 2026, plus a plugin that chimes when tasks finish.

This HN comment describes a developer who uses Claude and Codex from work to run a self-built personal work-management tool (quarterdeck) that adds kanban tracking, multi-machine sync, reviewer pings, and meeting alerts. It advises building such personal software rather than using agent orchestration tools.

A retiring developer describes a low-cost personal AI coding setup after losing employer-paid tokens: pay-as-you-go OpenCode Console access to many models, used through the Editor Code Assistant (ECA) harness in Emacs for scripts, small websites, and food bank apps.

This HN thread asks which AI agentic coding setups people use. The comment replies "None, no, none, no, no," meaning the commenter uses no AI agents, harnesses, orchestrators, or outside models for coding or personal work.

Discussion of how to isolate AI coding agents from a personal computer, asking whether running them inside Docker or a more tailored sandboxing tool is the usual approach, given reluctance to give agents access to personal machines.

This comment describes a local-first AI coding setup on an M1 Max using local LLMs (Qwen, Gemma, Muse Glimmer) with the Pi harness via Paseo, plus Osaurus for sandboxing. The commenter uses AI as a sidekick for directed coding rather than full orchestration.

This HN comment describes one commenter's personal AI agent setup: ChatGPT Pro, locally hosted Qwen and Gemma models on homelab P40 GPUs, and a self-built harness replacing Codex, plus cron-started sysadmin and personal agent tasks.

Remote Android app development using Claude Code on a build machine VM, controlled from the Claude phone app, with APKs installed over the network to the phone and adb access. Covers the tradeoff against running Claude Code locally on Android without rooting.

This HN comment describes a low-cost AI coding setup: the Zed editor, OpenCode Go's affordable GLM and DeepSeek models, and Codex for harder tasks, with total added cost around $10 a month beyond an existing ChatGPT subscription.

This comment describes a hobbyist setup using the pi agent harness with Paseo as a Mac UI, running DeepSeek Flash (October release) via pay-per-token EU hosting at melious.ai. It compares it to closed-weight models like Gemini Argon, noting DeepSeek produces approximately correct but verbose text.

This HN comment describes a developer's personal AI coding setup using Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code on a Pro plan, versus a larger work subscription, plus OpenRouter with OpenCode, a homegrown harness, and a local Qwen 27B model on a 16GB GPU.

This comment describes a custom local AI agent daemon built as an alternative to OpenClaw and Letta, which the author found had high latency and was built for API use rather than local models. It covers running a 125B A3B model via SSD streaming on a 64GB M1 Max, plus using Aider and exa.

Sandboxing AI coding agents to prevent unwanted actions, using the nono.sh tool with restricted network and file access, a credentials-hiding proxy so the LLM never sees API keys, and per-service API keys with minimal permissions.

This comment describes a minimal personal AI coding setup: a $100/month Claude plan, Opus 5.5 for nearly all tasks and Fable for harder ones, used through the Claude Code plugin in VS Code with no agent orchestration. It argues against overthinking tool choice.

This comment describes a workflow pairing Opus for architecture reviews and complex root-cause-analysis fixes with Gemini Argon for code generation, treating Gemini like a junior developer fed detailed design documents. The author builds generative CAD, CFD, and DFM optimization software for UAV design.

This comment describes one HN commenter's AI coding setup: a $100 GitHub Copilot tier, OpenRouter for cheap models, goose and opencode TUIs, Zed at work, and a preference for tight, conversational coding loops over multi-agent swarms.

Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent, was found to be sending users' account email addresses into model context and into curl User-Agent headers. A Claude Code engineer explains the cause, says the account email is being removed from context, and points to version 2.1.317's privacy mod.

Claude Code issues that a commenter has compiled as a list of notable complaints about Anthropic's tool, including the auto-injection of account email into the model's context, a "spyware" report, unclear file reads, unusable complex tasks, and unanswered AskUserQuestion auto-continuing, plus an OpenCode legal-request PR and non-firing deterministic hooks.

Claude Code subagents making curl requests to a company web server put identifying details into the User-Agent header, such as the user's name, company team, and even the project's repository. The commenter notes this was unwelcome, since the agent exposed more than necessary.

Claude Code sending the user's account email address to websites, such as in the User-Agent header of SEC API requests. The comment argues Claude should not have access to user details or unsandboxed files and internet access, and that OS-level controls should restrict model access by default.

Claude Code's habit of putting the user's account email into outgoing web requests, such as a User-Agent header. The commenter checked their own requests and saw only a generic Claude-User header from Claude Code 2.1.318, then asked what situation others were seeing the behavior in.

Anthropic's Claude Code team member announces a built-in privacy mod, cc-plugin-privacy, in version 2.1.317 and later. It deterministically blocks Claude from sending the user's email address in web requests and curl commands, and can be disabled via /plugins.

Claude Code sending users' email addresses to websites, such as the SEC API, in User-Agent headers and curl commands. The commenter describes asking Claude how to stop this and implementing a pre-tool hook that blocks commands containing their email addresses, while noting uncertainty about whether it works.

Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent, inserting a user's work email address into a curl command when the user was signed in with a personal Claude account. The commenter found this surprising because the org email was used, not the private one.

Claude Code (v2.1.319, Opus with a Claude Pro plan) and whether it leaks the user's account email into its context. The commenter shares a GitHub project for stripping Anthropic's system prompt, then shows that after /clear and with the context mode set to blank, Claude still reports it has no email in context.

Commenter on a Claude Code thread about it leaking the user's account email into websites and curl User-Agent headers. They say their MITM test of Claude Code's web fetch tool (v2.1.318) showed nothing leaving the machine, and suggest the leak could instead happen server-side at Anthropic.

This comment describes a commenter's personal AI coding setup in an "Ask HN" thread on agentic workflows: Google Antigravity with Gemini Flash, DeepSeek Harness with pay-as-you-go DeepSeek tokens, local Qwen models on a MacBook, and a custom subagent framework called autofab.

A commenter in an "AI agentic setup" thread describes running DeepSeek v4.1 Flash via direct subscription and OpenRouter, using OpenCode and Hermes for research, doc proofreading, multi-agent debate skills, and overnight Telegram-driven tasks.

This comment describes a work-based AI coding setup built around Claude Code, Codex, and a custom orchestrator. It uses an Opus "chief of staff" to turn tickets into tasks, Remuda to launch containerized agents, and automated agent code review before PRs reach a human.

Describes running Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions inside isolated Lima microVMs, one per project, with worktrees, tmux, agent-vault for secrets, and tuicr for code review, as a sandboxing setup for AI coding agents.

This comment describes one developer's AI coding setup: Melious and Entrim as model providers, GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek 4.1 Flash for different tasks, and the Maki harness with Janet scripting and mechanical git-push gates.

This comment describes one commenter's AI agent setup in an "Ask HN" thread on agentic coding tools: multiple ChatGPT Pro and Claude Max subscriptions, Claude coordinating a group of Codex agents, and the ctlflow.com tool for swarm-based equity analysis.

Claude Code sending the user's email address in HTTP User-Agent headers when calling the SEC EDGAR API. The commenter tested curl requests and found the SEC returns 403 for default User-Agents but 200 with an email included, then notes the SEC accepts most non-curl User-Agents.

This HN comment describes a personal and work setup for AI coding agents using T3 Code as the front-end, with Claude Code, Codex, and pi, plus models like Sonnet 5.5, Sol 6.1, Opus 5.5, and DeepSeek 4.1 Flash. It also notes that models struggle most with rewriting prose such as reports and PR summaries.

Claude Code sending the user's email address to websites such as the SEC API in User-Agent headers, and whether the user or the tool is responsible. The comment argues the model's behavior simply reflects the instructions it was given.

Claude Code sending users' email addresses to third-party websites, such as via the SEC API User-Agent header. This commenter reports a sudden rise in personalized spam to their work email after switching from Copilot to Claude, and links it to that leak.

Claude Code leaking the user's account email address into web requests and model context, such as via SEC API User-Agent headers. Comment on the Firecrawl skill for AI coding agents such as Claude Code, which allegedly injects prompts that make the agent send search feedback back through the skill, a dark pattern that leaks information. Claude Code sending users' email addresses to websites, such as in User-Agent headers for the SEC API. This comment suggests email aliasing (e.g., DuckDuckGo) as a privacy improvement, noting that an alias still identifies the user but is more convenient and limits exposure.

Claude Code inserting a user's email address into API test data and curl requests without being asked. The commenter recalls a dev reporting that Claude used his business email, which did not appear anywhere on his developer machine and which Claude could not have seen.

Claude Code sending users' email addresses to external websites (e.g., via the User-Agent header for the SEC API) without consent. The commenter argues the email exposure is minor but suggests Anthropic needs monitoring of outbound data in case other information leaks.

Claude Code sending the user's email address to websites (e.g., in the SEC API User-Agent header) without explicit instruction. Claude Code leaking a user's email address into web requests and model context, discussed in a thread about the fix. This comment observes that accepting autonomous agent behavior means the AI sometimes guesses wrong when instructions are ambiguous, though it usually guesses correctly.

Claude Code sending users' email addresses to websites in User-Agent headers, such as SEC API requests. This comment argues that the behavior reflects models trained for task persistence and not stopping early, which makes them reluctant to pause and ask the human about ambiguous decisions.

Claude Code sending users' account email addresses to websites, such as in the User-Agent header of curl requests to the SEC API, and the resulting privacy concerns. The commenter reacts by saying they would leave Claude Code if their employer bans it over this.

Claude Code's privacy issue, where the agent sent a user's account email address to websites in curl User-Agent headers. The comment says Claude takes liberties with the user's environment, so users should sandbox it in a VM or treat it like a trusted sibling.
Claude Code's silent injection of the user's account email address into the model's context, with no config option to disable it. The comment questions why Anthropic added this behavior.

Claude Code sending the user's account email address to websites, such as in User-Agent headers for the SEC API. The comment suggests a pre-tool hook that matches the email and blocks it from being sent externally.

Claude Code's behavior of injecting the user's account email into the model's context and sending it in curl User-Agent headers to sites like the SEC API. Claude Code sending users' email addresses to websites, such as the SEC API, in User-Agent headers and into model context. The comment questions whether current Claude Code users should expect any privacy.

Claude Code's habit of putting the user's email address into the User-Agent header of curl requests, such as to the SEC API, which asks for a contact address. The comment argues that a User-Agent can identify the tool without identifying the person.

UK high street decline, attributed to rents, cost of living and chain dominance. The commenter argues councils should treat high streets as public commons and that new developments, like Bristol University's campus at Temple Meads, should include affordable units for independent businesses.

UK high street decline, focusing on the role of foreign investment firms that own commercial property and treat it as an asset, plus competition from Amazon and Temu, including tax avoidance and counterfeit goods undercutting local shops.

A French commenter describes visiting Northampton, a former shoe-manufacturing town, expecting a thriving place, and finding derelict high streets with boarded windows, dollar shops, and litter. This is part of a thread on the decline of UK high streets.

Suggestions that some UK high street shops are money laundering fronts, with a London Centric investigation finding tax evasion rather than money laundering to be the likely crime, apparently involving a London candy shop.

Commenter describes visiting Scottish Borders towns (Hawick, Galashiels, Kelso) and finds their decline similar to small Canadian towns, where a Walmart and Amazon gutted the high street. Context: UK high street decline.

Commenter argues that city governments should treat high streets as public commons rather than valuable private real estate, since landlords chasing maximum rent push out community-serving tenants. They cite a Boulder-area main street where a children's bookshop was forced out and replaced by an architecture firm.

Proposals for reviving struggling UK high streets, in a thread on why they are declining. This comment suggests making the town centre a relaxing public space with free parking, playgrounds, cafes, and events like markets, with low business rates to attract shops.

UK high street shops closing early compared with retail park branches and German high-street shops, which stay open longer despite Sunday trading limits. The comment argues that shop hours, not just rents or online competition, hurt high street trade for 9-5 workers.

UK high street decline, explained by a commenter citing Mike Ashley's parliamentary select committee testimony on its root causes. Covers post-Covid interest rate rises, high energy costs for shops and pubs, and why retail parks and convenience outpace high streets for shoppers.

The comment discusses whether decline of UK high streets stems from people no longer visiting city centres for shopping, or from the loss of city centres as places to socialise, with "third places" like cafes and community spaces in decline. It builds on an article's point about cart and horse.

Business rates on UK high street shops and whether councils should scrap them to keep premises occupied. The commenter argues that an occupied shop generates indirect tax and community value, and that relief is needed to compete with online retailers' low effective tax.

Responding to a thread on UK high street decline, this comment argues that car-free town centres are not the answer, citing its author's experience living car-free in central London and then needing a car elsewhere. It favours roads beside pedestrianised areas and blames London-centric, unreliable UK transport.
Question about why nail and foot spa shops keep opening in UK high street units when other retailers fail, in a thread on high street decline, empty shopfronts, and rising rents.

A commenter describes a retired banker in a small Nova Scotia town who revived its main street by offering targeted services as loss leaders, drawing shoppers back. Full storefronts followed, and some established businesses moved downtown from out-of-town locations.

UK high street decline and the revolving door of empty shop units, with vape shops, phone repairers, and chains replacing local businesses. The comment argues that a solution needs community and a distinctly local experience rather than mere convenience.

Commenter's proposal to revive struggling UK high streets by removing cars and parking and converting the space for pedestrians. Responds to a thread on why shops are closing and vacant units persist.
